documents: Yang et al. 2022, Glacier Surface Speed Variations on the Kenai Peninsula, Alaska, 2014-2019, JGR Earth Surface 127, e2022JF006599 (published PDF, 22 pages)

entry.evidence: However, the spatial or temporal coverage of these data on the Kenai Peninsula is insufficient to analyze the spatiotemporal variations in detail.

steps.action: Posed the aim: characterize the seasonal and interannual ice-flow variations of all Kenai Peninsula glaciers, focusing on terminus type and on GLOF effects.
steps.quote: We focus on differences between tidewater, lake-, and land-terminating glaciers

steps.action: Acquired 92 Sentinel-1A/B SLC TOPS image pairs covering October 2014 to December 2019, plus a TerraSAR-X pair and the IFSAR DEM.
steps.quote: We used 92 pairs of Sentinel-1A and 1B single-look complex (SLC) SAR TOPS images between October 2014 and December 2019

steps.action: Derived surface speed fields on a 90 m grid by intensity offset tracking in GAMMA, then built an error budget from coregistration, tracking and ionosphere terms.
steps.quote: We applied SAR offset tracking using 93 Sentinel-1 images to derive 92 surface speed fields

steps.action: Compared Sentinel-1 speeds pixel by pixel with TerraSAR-X-derived speeds over Bear Glacier for an overlapping 2016 period, giving a mean difference of 8.6 m/a.
steps.quote: Sentinel-1 results agree well with the TerraSAR-X ice speeds in most parts of the main branch of the glacier

steps.action: Generated annual and seasonal mean speed fields by error-weighted averaging, with propagated uncertainty and a 70% temporal-coverage threshold.
steps.quote: Annual and seasonal surface ice speed fields were generated from the error-weighted average of all ice speed fields

steps.action: Described the spatial pattern of 5-year mean speed: 9-600 m/a, regional mean 69 m/a, fastest at tidewater termini, higher on the coastal side.
steps.quote: Ice flow speeds were generally higher on the coastal side (east)

steps.action: Compared centerline speed profiles by terminus type with expectations: land-terminating maxima near the median elevation, tidewater maxima near the terminus.
steps.quote: As expected, land-terminating glaciers have their speed maxima around the median elevation

steps.action: Computed seasonal enhancement factors per pixel and established a spring speedup about 50% above the annual mean almost everywhere.
steps.quote: Most strikingly, the spring speeds are equal or greater than the annual mean almost everywhere.

steps.action: Repeated the seasonal analysis as monthly enhancement factors at two sites on each of 77 glaciers grouped by terminus type, and found a coherent pattern.
steps.quote: a coherent seasonal pattern is obvious for both sites regardless of terminus type

steps.action: Built annual maps for 2015-2019 and monthly speed series by terminus type, and established synchronous monthly variation with no trend in annual means.
steps.quote: revealing no significant interannual variation in the spatial pattern

steps.action: Set the observed seasonal cycle against published seasonal speed patterns from Alaska, Greenland and Svalbard.
steps.quote: consistent with observations on many other glaciers

steps.action: Adopted the published subglacial drainage-evolution account (distributed to channelized system) to explain the spring peak and the fall secondary peak.
steps.quote: These seasonal variations are associated with changes in basal motion as meltwater input varies

steps.action: Proposed glacier size and thickness, frontal ablation and coastal mass turnover as explanations for the faster flow of lake- and tidewater glaciers.
steps.quote: Part of the differences can be attributed to differences in glacier size (and associated thickness).

steps.action: Argued that the synchronous monthly behavior is not a processing artifact, because coregistration succeeded with no visible phase jumps.
steps.quote: This behavior cannot be explained by errors in the processing chain

steps.action: Hypothesized that regional-scale meteorological drivers of water input control the synchronous monthly variations.
steps.quote: the monthly speed variations are controlled by regional-scale meteorological drivers

steps.action: Correlated annual mean speed with summer precipitation and temperature at weather stations: no precipitation correlation and a weak negative temperature correlation, with caveats.
steps.quote: We found no correlation between annual mean speed and summer precipitation averaged over six weather stations

steps.action: Used NPS time-lapse camera records of the 2018 and 2019 Bear Glacier GLOFs to fix the event timing within the study period.
steps.quote: A time lapse camera installed in June 2017 by the Kenai Fjords NPS recorded the onset and duration of two GLOFs

steps.action: Compared speed time series above and below the ice-dammed lake (400 m contour), and found a roughly threefold speedup below the lake during the 2019 GLOF.
steps.quote: the area below the ice-dammed lake accelerated strongly, reaching speeds roughly three times the average flow speed

steps.action: Excluded a weather cause for the 2019 acceleration, since no unusual temperature or precipitation was recorded nearby.
steps.quote: no unusual temperature or precipitation events were recorded at a nearby weather station during the GLOF

steps.action: Found that the 2018 GLOF produced no short-term speed response, and suggested a developed channelized drainage system or smaller lake volume.
steps.quote: the Bear Glacier GLOF in 2018 had a negligible impact on flow speed

steps.action: Hypothesized that the 2018 GLOF triggered a longer-term speedup of the lowest ~8 km through a breach of the moraine barrier.
steps.quote: the GLOF in 2018 seems to be the trigger for a longer-term speed-up of the glacier in the terminus area

steps.action: Documented with Sentinel-2 images, airplane observations and NPS information the persistent breach, ocean inflow, 1.1 km retreat and tripled thinning.
steps.quote: the moraine breach in August 2018 persisted at least throughout 2019 as evident from Sentinel-2 images

steps.action: Added terminus buoyancy, facilitated by greater salinity, as an amplifying mechanism for the Bear Glacier acceleration.
steps.quote: it is also possible that part of the glacier terminus became buoyant thus amplifying the flow acceleration

steps.action: Kept the GLOF-induced breach and the resulting proglacial lake changes as the likely trigger of the Bear Glacier speedup, noting that direct observations are lacking.
steps.quote: Direct observations would be needed to provide conclusive explanations for the speedup at Bear Glacier

steps.action: Checked two Skilak Glacier lake drainages detected in Landsat images and found no flow acceleration; noted the long averaging periods.
steps.quote: We did not find any flow acceleration associated with the lake drainage

steps.action: Observed a step-like ~50% terminus speedup at Ellsworth Glacier after a 2016 retreat, with rift formation and tabular iceberg detachment seen in Landsat and Sentinel-2 images.
steps.quote: A notable step-like speedup of the terminus region during the study period is also observed at lake-terminating Ellsworth Glacier

steps.action: Hypothesized that the Ellsworth terminus became buoyant in 2016 because the speedup preceded the calving event.
steps.quote: we hypothesize that part of the terminus region became buoyant in 2016

steps.action: Compared the results with published speed data sets (Burgess et al. 2013, ITS_LIVE, GoLIVE): spatial patterns agree, ITS_LIVE magnitudes differ.
steps.quote: We compare our results to previously published glacier speed data sets

steps.action: Kept the regional regularities: speed differences by terminus type, spring speedup, synchronous monthly variation and no interannual trend over 2014-2019.
steps.quote: We find significant differences in the spatial and temporal speed variations between glaciers of different terminus type.

Checked against TerraSAR-X, stable terrain and published data sets; parameters not varied

end.claim: Over 2014-2019 on the Kenai Peninsula, lake- and tidewater glaciers flow 1.7 and 2.3 times faster than land-terminating glaciers, speeds peak in spring (about 50% above the annual mean), and monthly variations are synchronous across terminus types with no interannual trend.

decisive_move.sentence: Deriving 92 regional speed fields by Sentinel-1 intensity offset tracking produced the data set on which every regularity and event analysis rests.

gates.evidence: All available Sentinel-1 pairs were processed without a guiding hypothesis (p. 2-3). The speed product faced a TerraSAR-X comparison it could have failed (p. 5). The GLOF attribution faced an upper vs lower area comparison and a weather check (p. 13). The terminus-type regularities were not tested against stated rivals. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Normalized median absolute deviation as a robust alternative to the standard deviation (Rousseeuw & Croux 1993)
Patch intensity cross-correlation (offset tracking) of C-band and X-band SAR images, GAMMA software

novelty_claims.quote: with unprecedented spatial and temporal resolution and coverage for the 3,900 km2

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The validation rests on one TerraSAR-X pair over one glacier, with 11 days of overlap against a 54-day Sentinel pair. Processing parameters (window size, SNR threshold of 6.0, filter) were taken from prior studies and not varied, so no robustness check is performed. Some error terms are assumed or neglected: ionosphere for TerraSAR-X, DEM surface lowering, water vapour and tides. The weather correlation is reported inconsistently: p. 12 gives a weak significant negative correlation with summer temperature, while p. 18 says no correlation was found. Sub-claims sit at other statuses. The speed fields are estimate_with_resolution (about 10% uncertainty). The Bear Glacier GLOF and moraine-breach attribution and the Ellsworth buoyancy attribution are best_explanation; the authors say direct observations are needed. The seasonal drainage mechanism is cited, not tested. Inference: the GLOF analyses were not planned at acquisition but followed from noticed anomalies and NPS camera records.

disagreements.support: ITS_LIVE gives a lower domain mean (40 vs 64 m/a) but tidewater maxima almost three times higher than the Sentinel-1 results; the paper cites Friedl et al. (2021) for similar overestimates at glacier fronts.
disagreements.quote: This is consistent with observations on Svalbard by Friedl et al. (2021) who also found higher ITS_LIVE speeds over glacier fronts and shear zones.

disagreements.target: GoLIVE (Scambos et al., 2016) and ITS_LIVE global velocity data sets
disagreements.support: Their spatial or temporal coverage of the Kenai Peninsula is too sparse for detailed spatiotemporal analysis; GoLIVE covers less than 30% of the glaciers.
disagreements.quote: However, the spatial or temporal coverage of these data on the Kenai Peninsula is insufficient to analyze the spatiotemporal variations in detail.

disagreements.target: Burgess et al. (2013) flow map of Central Alaska glaciers
disagreements.support: The earlier map used winter images only and has 64% coverage; its spatial pattern agrees with the new results, and winter speeds are shown to approximate annual means.
disagreements.quote: but speeds were based on winter images only

alternatives_considered.reason: DInSAR is limited by decorrelation in regions of rapid and incoherent flow

alternatives_considered.chosen: Median and normalized median absolute deviation for coregistration error
alternatives_considered.reason: The coregistration error is not normally distributed
